title: Design, implement, integrate, and manage extension/development projects and programmes

lessons.title: Projects, programmes and the design process
lessons.html:
Projects and programmes in agricultural development

A project is a time-bound set of activities with a defined budget and specific results, for example establishing a 20 ha drip-irrigated vegetable scheme for a cooperative over two years. A programme is a group of related projects and ongoing activities managed together toward a broader goal, such as a provincial smallholder commercialisation programme that includes irrigation, mechanisation, mentorship and market access projects across several districts.

At this level, the practitioner is expected to design interventions that are strategically sound, technically feasible, financially viable, socially acceptable and environmentally sustainable, and to integrate them with other development efforts.

The project cycle

  1. Identification: needs, opportunities and alignment with policy, such as provincial agricultural strategies and municipal Integrated Development Plans.
  2. Design and appraisal: feasibility, logical framework, budget, risk and stakeholder analysis.
  3. Approval and financing: securing funds and formal authority.
  4. Implementation: mobilising resources, delivering activities, managing contracts.
  5. Monitoring and evaluation: tracking progress and measuring results and impact.
  6. Closure and handover: transferring assets and responsibilities to beneficiaries or other institutions, and documenting lessons.

Feasibility appraisal

DimensionKey questions
TechnicalAre soils, water, climate and technology suitable? Is there a reliable water use authorisation where needed?
Financial and economicDo projected cash flows cover operating costs, replacement of equipment and a return to members? What is the sensitivity to price and yield shocks?
MarketWho will buy, at what price, standard and volume? Are there letters of intent or contracts?
InstitutionalAre governance, land tenure and management capacity adequate?
SocialWho benefits and who may be excluded? Is there genuine demand?
EnvironmentalWhat are the effects on soil, water and biodiversity? Is environmental authorisation required?

Many failed land reform and smallholder projects in South Africa were technically designed but weak on markets, institutions or operating finance. Rigorous appraisal across all dimensions is the main defence against this.

lessons.title: Logical frameworks, theory of change and planning tools
lessons.html:
Structuring the design

Theory of change

A theory of change explains how and why the intervention is expected to lead to the desired change. It sets out the causal pathway and the assumptions behind each step. For example: if growers receive irrigation infrastructure, technical mentorship and a supply contract, and if water supply is reliable and members cooperate, then production volumes and quality will meet buyer standards, leading to sustained sales and increased household income.

The logical framework

The logframe summarises the design in a matrix.

LevelExampleIndicatorAssumption
GoalImproved livelihoods of member householdsHousehold income from farmingMacro-economic stability
PurposeCooperative supplies vegetables profitably to formal marketsAnnual sales volume and net marginBuyer maintains contract
OutputsIrrigation installed; members trained; food safety system in placeHectares irrigated; members certified; audit passedReliable electricity and water
ActivitiesProcure system, run training, set up packshedBudget spent per planTimely release of funds

Indicators must be specific and measurable, with a baseline and target. Means of verification, such as sales records or audit reports, show where evidence will come from.

Implementation planning tools

  • Work breakdown structure: dividing the project into manageable work packages.
  • Gantt chart and critical path: scheduling activities and identifying those that cannot slip without delaying the project, such as installing irrigation before the planting window.
  • Budget and cash flow plan: capital, operating and contingency costs per period.
  • Responsibility matrix: who is responsible, accountable, consulted and informed for each task.
  • Risk register: risk, likelihood, impact, mitigation and owner.
  • Procurement plan: what is bought, by which method, and when, following applicable supply chain rules.

Participatory design

Beneficiaries should take part in design, not only receive the result. Participatory planning improves fit, ownership and later sustainability, and reveals assumptions that outsiders miss, such as labour availability during school holidays or conflict over land allocation.

lessons.title: Implementing, integrating and managing programmes
lessons.html:
Managing implementation

Implementation requires a governance structure, such as a project steering committee with representatives of beneficiaries, funders, government and technical partners, and a project manager responsible for daily delivery.

Core management disciplines

  • Scope management: control changes through a formal change request process.
  • Schedule and cost control: compare actual progress and spending against the baseline monthly, and act early on variances.
  • Contract management: clear specifications, payment against verified deliverables and documented inspections, for example before paying an irrigation contractor.
  • Risk and issue management: update the risk register and escalate issues beyond the manager's authority.
  • Stakeholder communication: regular, honest reporting to beneficiaries, partners and funders.
  • Financial accountability: compliance with funder conditions and, for public funds, the Public Finance Management Act.

Integration

Development projects fail when they operate in isolation. Integration means aligning the project with other initiatives and services so that each component supports the others. Examples include aligning with the municipal Integrated Development Plan for roads and electricity, coordinating with the Department of Water and Sanitation on water use authorisation, linking with financiers for production credit, connecting with commodity organisations for mentorship, and with buyers for market access. Sequencing matters: infrastructure without training, or production without a market, wastes resources.

Programme management

At programme level the manager focuses on portfolio performance: allocating resources among projects, managing interdependencies, standardising tools and reporting, capturing shared lessons and reviewing whether the programme still serves its strategic goal. Projects that are not viable should be redesigned or closed rather than funded indefinitely.

Sustainability and exit

Plan the exit from the design stage: build beneficiary management capacity, establish asset ownership and maintenance funds, secure ongoing market and support links, and hand over in phases. Evaluate outcomes and, where possible, impact some time after closure.

Key points

  • Use the project cycle and appraise technical, financial, market, institutional, social and environmental feasibility.
  • Express the design through a theory of change and logframe with measurable indicators and explicit assumptions.
  • Control scope, schedule, cost, contracts and risk through formal governance.
  • Integrate projects with municipal, sectoral, financial and market partners and sequence components correctly.
  • Design for sustainability and a phased exit from the start.
